questions._flag: SPLIT-TOPIC question, filed on the heavier half, flagged so the choice is visible rather than implied. Part (i) (1 mark) is refraction and the wave nature of light — Wave Optics / 'Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves' would fit it; part (ii) (2 marks: identify the radiation + two uses) is squarely Electromagnetic Waves / 'Electromagnetic Spectrum'. Filed on the EM-spectrum half because it carries 2 of the 3 marks, matching how the identical question is filed on the opener 55/1/1 (its Q11a). SEPARATELY, worth knowing for the later solution-authoring step: \(1.0 \times 10^{11}\) Hz (~3 mm) sits on the microwave / far-infrared boundary, and the marking scheme (ms p06) accordingly accepts THREE different identifications — 'Infrared/ Microwaves/ Radio waves' — listing uses for each. That is answer latitude on a subjective row, not a defect and not an unconditional award, so it is recorded here rather than in _cbseVoided.

questions.context: The principle of superposition is used to understand the phenomenon of interference of light waves. The principle states that at a particular point, the resultant displacement produced by a number of waves is the vector sum of the displacements produced by each wave. Light waves from two coherent sources produce interference pattern. Thomas Young devised a way to obtain two coherent sources using two identical pinholes (\(S_1\) and \(S_2\)) illuminated by a single monochromatic pinhole source S. Using these sources in his experiment known as Young's double slit experiment, Young studied the interference pattern. The pattern consists of alternate bright and dark fringes. The distance between two successive bright or dark finges depends on the distance between \(S_1\) and \(S_2\), the distance of the screen from the plane of \(S_1S_2\) and the wavelength of light used.
questions.stem:
Consider the following waves :
(i) \(y_1 = a \sin \omega t\)
(ii) \(y_2 = a \sin 2\omega t\)
(iii) \(y_3 = a \sin (2\omega t + \phi)\)
(iv) \(y_4 = a \sin \left(4\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\)
Which pair of the waves coming from two sources \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) will produce interference ?
questions._flag: TWO THINGS, both about this paper's Section C. (1) THE PRINTED PASSAGE CARRIES A TYPO, transcribed as printed: 'dark finges' (for 'fringes') in the last sentence. Not corrected — the context is the faithful record and feeds content_hash. (2) THIS PAPER HAS FIVE KEYED MCQs, contradicting the `wave.ts` key column, which prints 'n/a (no MCQs)' for it. All five were taken from there verbatim — I (B), II (C), III (D), IV (C), V (C) — read off the rendered page AND confirmed against the scheme PDF's own text layer, which agrees character for character. questions.stem:
Consider the effect on the angular separation of the fringes in a Young's double slit experiment due to the following operations :
(i) the screen is moved away from the plane of the slits,
(ii) the separation between the two slits is increased till fringes are observed.
Which of the following options is correct ?

options.label: A
options.text: It remains constant in both cases.

options.label: C
options.text: It remains constant in (i) but decreases in (ii).

options.label: D
options.text: It decreases in (i) but remains constant in (ii).

questions._flag: SUSPECTED DROPPED WORD IN THE PRINTED STEM, transcribed as printed and NOT corrected — reported for the maintainer to adjudicate. Operation (ii) reads 'the separation between the two slits is increased till fringes are observed'. The NCERT exercise this is drawn from reads 'till fringes are NOT observed' (increasing d shrinks the fringe width until the pattern can no longer be resolved), and as printed the clause is close to vacuous, since fringes are observed to begin with. Confirmed at 3x on idx 10 that no 'not' is present. THE KEY IS UNAFFECTED EITHER WAY: angular separation is \(\lambda/d\), which is independent of screen distance and decreases when d is increased, so option (C) is correct under both readings — which is why this is a wording flag and not a defect that changes the answer. The opener 55/1/1 prints the identical clause, so it is a series-wide typesetting slip rather than a one-off.
